scope_note: Per the 2026 Grade 11 ATP, this is a Term 1 topic (Weeks 4-8, before the June exam) covering: (1) complete the square; (2) solve quadratic equations by factorisation and by the quadratic formula; (3) solve quadratic inequalities in one unknown, interpreted graphically; (4) equations in two unknowns, one linear and one quadratic; (5) nature of roots. It is examined in Paper 1 (the ATP's Paper 1 topic list groups it under 'Algebraic expressions, equations and inequalities', 45 of 150 marks). Because this is Term 1 content, May/June mid-year papers and March common tests legitimately examine it (same situation as the Term 1 Trigonometry reduction/equations topic) -- there is no pacing exclusion. Surd equations, exponential equations, and other content belonging to the 'Exponents and Surds' ATP topic were excluded throughout, even when they appeared alongside this topic's content in the same Question 1, to avoid double-counting against that separate knowledge base.

archetypes.name: Solve a quadratic equation by factorisation
archetypes.description: Solve a quadratic equation for x by factorising it into two linear factors and applying the zero-product law. Presentation varies: sometimes already given in factored form (e.g. 'x(2x+6)=0'), sometimes needing rearrangement to standard form first, and occasionally as a difference-of-squares special case (e.g. 'x²-100=0').

typical_breakdown: A1: correct factors (or correct rearrangement to standard form if not pre-factored)
A1 (or A1+A1): both value(s) of x
marking_pattern.consensus: Consistent across all 13 examples -- one mark for the factorisation/rearrangement step, one or two marks for the answer(s).
marking_pattern.notes: One example (KZN June 2026, x²-100=0) is a difference-of-squares special case; its memo accepts an alternative method of isolating x² and taking square roots of both sides as equally valid.

archetypes.language_notes: Almost always phrased as 'Solve for x:' as a lead-in to a sub-list of parts 1.1.1, 1.1.2, etc.

archetypes.name: Solve a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula, rounded to two decimal places
archetypes.description: Solve a quadratic equation whose roots are irrational, using the quadratic formula, with the answer required correct to two decimal places. Sometimes the equation must first be rearranged to standard form or cleared of a fraction before the formula is applied.
command_verbs_used: Solve for x ... (correct to TWO decimal places)

typical_breakdown: A1: standard form (if rearrangement needed)
A1 (CA): correct substitution into the quadratic formula
A1+A1 (CA): the two answers
marking_pattern.notes: An explicit memo instruction appears in nearly every source: 'Penalise ONE mark for incorrect rounding, in this question ONLY.' One example (KZN June 2026, '3x-5=3/x') requires clearing a fraction to reach standard form first, rather than a simple rearrangement.

archetypes.language_notes: The parenthetical instruction '(correct to TWO decimal places)' or '(answer correct to TWO decimal places)' is used verbatim across nearly all sources.

archetypes.name: Solve a quadratic inequality already reducible to standard/factored form
archetypes.description: Solve a quadratic inequality where the expression is either already factored or already in simple standard form (ax²+bx+c compared to 0), requiring only factorisation, critical values, and sign-diagram or sketch-based interval selection.

typical_breakdown: A1: correct factors
A1 (CA): critical values (accepted if shown on a sketch or number line)
A1+A1 (CA): the final answer, both bounds
marking_pattern.notes: One example (Nov 2021 Q1.3.2, 'x²+8x+16>0') is a perfect-square edge case where the solution is 'all reals except one point' rather than an interval -- the memo explicitly requires both criteria (x∈R AND x≠-4) for the answer mark, a genuinely different-shaped answer from the rest of this archetype's evidence.

archetypes.language_notes: Answers are accepted either as a compound inequality (e.g. '-11<x<-8') or in interval notation (e.g. 'x∈(-11;-8)'); memos consistently accept both forms interchangeably.

archetypes.name: Solve a quadratic inequality requiring expansion or rearrangement before standard form
archetypes.description: Solve a quadratic inequality where the expression must first be expanded (e.g. a product of two binomials compared to a nonzero constant) or rearranged/factored by grouping before it can be reduced to standard form and solved.

typical_breakdown: A1: standard form after expansion
A1 (CA): correct factors
A1+A1 (CA): the answer, both parts
marking_pattern.notes: Two memos (Nov 2021 and Nov 2023) explicitly penalise a mark for writing 'AND' instead of 'OR' between disjoint solution branches (or vice versa for a single compound interval) -- this OR/AND distinction is treated strictly. One example (Nov 2025 Q1.1.3, 'x(x-4)+2(4-x)>0') requires factoring by grouping rather than simple expansion, a slightly less routine variant.

archetypes.language_notes: Where the solution set is two disjoint rays, the answer is written with 'or' between them (e.g. 'x<-3 or x>5'); memos are strict that 'and' is incorrect there.

archetypes.name: Solve a system of equations simultaneously, one linear and one quadratic in two unknowns
archetypes.description: Solve for x and y given one linear and one quadratic (or quadratic-shaped) equation, by making one variable the subject of the linear equation and substituting into the second, reducing to a quadratic in one variable. Includes variants where the second equation is given in a 'messier' unexpanded form, as a product-form equation (e.g. '(x-y)(5y-3x)=0'), or where a homogeneous-ratio shortcut is available.
command_verbs_used: Solve simultaneously for x and y

typical_breakdown: A1: one variable made the subject of the linear equation
A1 (CA): substitution into the second equation
A1 (CA): standard form
A1 (CA): factors
A1+A1 (CA): both values of each variable
marking_pattern.consensus: Consistent across most examples; several memos explicitly offer 'any other valid method' as an alternative route (e.g. solving for the other variable first).
marking_pattern.notes: One example (KZN Jun 2024 Q1.3) presents the second equation in product form '(x-y)(5y-3x)=0', which can be solved either by direct substitution or by first solving the product-form equation for one variable in terms of the other -- both methods appear in the memo. One example (Jun 2019 Q1.2) is preceded by a homogeneous-ratio step (finding x/y from a homogeneous quadratic relation) before the linear constraint is applied.

archetypes.language_notes: Consistently phrased as 'Solve for x and y' or 'Solve simultaneously for x and y', with the two equations given as a numbered pair.

archetypes.name: Reduce a non-standard equation to a quadratic via a structural technique (rational equation with LCD, or substitution of a repeated expression)
archetypes.description: Solve an equation that is not immediately quadratic in form -- either a rational equation with a factorable quadratic denominator (solved via LCD), an equation containing a repeated sub-expression that can be replaced by a single substituted variable (e.g. letting k=x²-2x, or u=x²), or two structurally identical equations where a known root of one directly yields an unknown in the other via the matching substitution. All variants reduce to a standard quadratic equation as the key intermediate step, often followed by a rejection of an extraneous or restricted value.
command_verbs_used: Determine the value of t/y ... hence

typical_breakdown: A1/M1: correct method or factorisation of denominator/recognition of the substitution
A1 (CA): standard form after substitution or LCD
A1 (CA): factors
A1 (CA): answer(s), with rejection of any restricted or extraneous value where applicable
marking_pattern.consensus: The mechanic (reduce to quadratic, then back-substitute or reject) is consistent, though the specific technique varies by example -- rational-equation LCD (2 examples), same-equation substitution of a repeated expression (2 examples, one of which is a biquadratic via u=x²), and cross-equation structural substitution using a previously-found root (2 examples).
marking_pattern.notes: This archetype deliberately groups several structurally-related but individually low-evidence techniques (each with only 1-2 examples alone) under one umbrella, since they share the same core skill of recognising and executing a substitution to reach a solvable quadratic. Anne-Marie may wish to review whether these should eventually be split into finer sub-archetypes once more evidence accumulates for each.

archetypes.language_notes: Rational-equation variants restate the LCD explicitly; substitution variants often use 'let k=...' or 'let u=...' in the memo even when the question paper does not suggest it.

archetypes.name: Determine or prove the nature of the roots of a (often parametric) quadratic equation
archetypes.description: Use the discriminant (or, in some variants, the sum/product of roots) to determine or prove a stated property of a quadratic equation's roots: non-real, equal, real, real-and-unequal (sometimes proved for all values of a parameter), real-rational-and-unequal, opposite in sign, or equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. Some variants ask for a parameter value or range; others ask for a general proof valid for all real values of a parameter; one variant asks for the roots to be left in symbolic quadratic-formula form before a follow-up question asks for a specific condition.
command_verbs_used: Discuss the nature of the roots
Determine the value(s) of p for which the roots are equal
Prove that ... the roots are non-real/real and unequal
Determine the value(s) of m for which the equation has real roots
For which value(s) will the equation have roots opposite in sign / equal in magnitude but opposite in sign

typical_breakdown: A1 (CA): substitution into the discriminant Δ=b²-4ac
A1 (CA): simplified expression for Δ
A1 (CA): the condition applied to Δ (=0, ≥0, or an inequality)
A1 (CA): the final answer or conclusion
marking_pattern.consensus: The discriminant mechanic is consistent, but the specific condition applied (and hence the final answer's shape) varies considerably across the 11 examples -- this is a topic-wide skill with many distinct question shapes rather than one repeated pattern.
marking_pattern.notes: Two general 'prove for all real p' proofs (Nov 2021 Q1.5, Jun 2023 Q1.4) were classified as Problem Solving (Level 4) rather than Complex, since they require a non-routine general argument about a parameter rather than a specific numeric answer -- Anne-Marie may want to sanity-check this classification. One example (Nov 2022 Q1.5.2, 'real, rational and unequal') has a memo that only checks Δ>0, without an explicit separate check that Δ is a perfect square (the actual requirement for rational roots) -- flagged as a possible memo gap, not a genuine disagreement in the pattern.

archetypes.language_notes: 'Discuss' is used once (Nov 2019) where other papers use 'Determine'; the shorthand 'Δ' for the discriminant is used throughout memos even when question papers write it out.

archetypes.name: Real-world word problem reducing to a quadratic equation
archetypes.description: A word problem (numbers with a given sum and product, ages with a fractional relationship, or a fencing/area optimisation) that must be translated into one or two equations and solved, generally reducing to a quadratic equation. The optimisation variant explicitly uses completing the square, directly matching the ATP's 'complete the square' skill.
command_verbs_used: Determine the value of the two numbers
Calculate the dimensions ... to obtain the maximum enclosed area

typical_breakdown: A1: setting up the equation(s) from the word description
A1 (CA): substitution
A1 (CA): standard form / completing the square
A1+A1 (CA): the final answer(s)
marking_pattern.consensus: The translate-then-solve mechanic is consistent across all three examples.
marking_pattern.notes: One example (Jun 2023 Q1.5) is worth 7 marks and uses completing the square explicitly rather than factorisation or the formula, matching the ATP's item 1 directly; the other two are worth 4-5 marks and reduce to a straightforward quadratic. One example (KZN Jun 2026 Q1.3, natural-number-constrained maximum of xy) is a related but distinct optimisation flavour and was excluded from this archetype's evidence count -- see excluded_archetypes.

archetypes.language_notes: Word problems in this topic are self-contained short paragraphs, occasionally illustrated (e.g. a family image for the ages problem).

style_profile.typical_sequencing: This topic is almost always Question 1 of Paper 1. It typically opens with a run of 'Solve for x' sub-questions moving from simplest to hardest (factorable equation, then quadratic formula, then a quadratic inequality, with surd/exponential equations from the separate Exponents and Surds topic often interleaved in the same numbered list), then moves to a simultaneous linear-quadratic system, and closes with either a nature-of-roots question or a word problem -- generally the most demanding sub-question in Q1.
style_profile.scaffolding_pattern: Sub-questions frequently build on each other via 'hence' or by reusing a previously-found value (e.g. a found root substituted into a structurally identical second equation, or a discriminant expression from part (a) reused in part (b) to find equal roots). Many multi-mark items show two full alternative memo methods side by side, explicitly credited as equally valid.
style_profile.notation_conventions: The instruction '(correct to TWO decimal places)' or '(answer correct to TWO decimal places)' is used verbatim wherever the quadratic formula gives irrational roots, paired with an explicit memo penalty for incorrect rounding, applied only to that specific sub-question. Inequality answers are accepted as either a compound inequality or interval notation; memos are strict that disjoint (outside-root) solution branches must be joined with 'OR', never 'AND', and vice versa for a single compound (between-root) interval.
